title: Tree: Huffman Decoding
directAnswer: Decode by walking the prebuilt Huffman tree one bit at a time: start at the root, go LEFT on '0' and RIGHT on '1'. Because Huffman codes are prefix-free, every codeword ends exactly at a leaf — so the moment you land on a leaf, append its character and reset back to the root. Repeat until the bit string is consumed. It's O(L) time in the length of the encoded string and O(1) extra space; the tree does all the disambiguation for you.

remember.pattern: Walk the Huffman tree per bit; emit at each leaf, reset to root
rules: '0' goes **left**, '1' goes **right** — the convention the tree was built with.
A node is a **leaf** when both children are null; only leaves carry real characters.
On reaching a leaf, **emit its character and reset to the root** for the next codeword.
Huffman codes are **prefix-free**, so a leaf is reached at exactly one unambiguous point — no backtracking.
Don't try to emit at internal nodes; their `data` is a placeholder, not an output character.
whenToUse: Decoding a bit stream against a known prefix-code (Huffman) tree
Any decode where the dictionary is structured as a trie/binary tree
Walking a tree driven by an external sequence of left/right instructions
antiSignals: You must BUILD the Huffman tree from frequencies → that's the encoding/priority-queue problem, not this
Codes are fixed-length → index directly, no tree walk needed
Codes are not prefix-free → tree decoding is ambiguous; a different scheme is required
remember.takeaway: Huffman decoding is a guided tree walk: the bits are turnstile instructions, leaves are output points, and the prefix-free property guarantees you always know exactly when a character ends. Reset to the root after every emit and the whole thing is one clean pass.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can drive a tree traversal from an external bit string, detect leaves correctly, and exploit the prefix-free property to decode unambiguously in one pass.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to reset to the root after emitting a character, mis-detecting leaves (emitting at internal nodes), or swapping the 0=left / 1=right convention.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY no backtracking is needed (prefix-free codes end at leaves), keep the walk to O(1) space, and contrast with the encoding side (building the tree from a min-heap).

problemStatement:
You are given the `root` of a prebuilt **Huffman tree** and an encoded binary string `s`. In the tree, every leaf stores one original character; internal nodes are structural placeholders. The encoding assigns each character the sequence of left/right turns ('0' = left, '1' = right) from the root to its leaf.

**Decode** `s` back into the original string and print it.
constraints: The Huffman tree is already built and valid (prefix-free)
Every leaf holds exactly one character; internal nodes hold a placeholder
'0' means go left, '1' means go right
understanding: Treat the bit string as step-by-step directions through the tree. Each bit moves you one edge down; whenever you arrive at a leaf you've completed one character's codeword, so you output that character and jump back to the root to start decoding the next one. The prefix-free property of Huffman codes is what makes 'stop at the first leaf' always correct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree already built, or do I build it from frequencies?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Already built. This is the decode side. Building the tree from character frequencies with a min-heap is the separate encoding problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How do I know a node is a leaf?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both children are null. Only leaves carry real characters; internal nodes have a placeholder value you must not emit.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which direction is 0 and which is 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By convention '0' goes left and '1' goes right. The tree was encoded with that convention, so decoding must match it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why don't I need to look ahead or backtrack?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Huffman codes are prefix-free: no codeword is a prefix of another. So the first leaf you hit is unambiguously the end of exactly one character — no lookahead required.

approaches.name: Tree Walk — One Bit at a Time, Reset at Leaves (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Lead with it — it's O(L) time, O(1) space, and uses the tree directly.
hints: Think of each bit as a single instruction: which child do you move to on '0' vs '1'?
Keep a pointer at the root and move it down one edge per bit. When does a codeword end?
A codeword ends at a leaf (both children null). Emit the leaf's character, reset the pointer to the root, and continue with the next bit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the L bits causes exactly one pointer move and O(1) leaf check → O(L) time. Only a single node pointer and the output buffer are used → O(1) auxiliary space (excluding the output itself).
approaches.explanation:
Decoding is a guided descent where the *input string*, not the tree's own structure, decides the path.

**Bits are directions.** Start with a pointer at the root. Read the bits left to right: on `'0'` move to the left child, on `'1'` move to the right child. Each bit advances the pointer one edge deeper.

**Leaves are emit points.** Internal nodes are just junctions; only leaves hold real characters. The moment the pointer lands on a leaf (both children null), one full codeword has been traced from root to leaf — so append that leaf's character to the output and **reset the pointer to the root** to begin the next character.

**Why no ambiguity or backtracking.** Huffman codes are *prefix-free*: no character's codeword is a prefix of another's. Structurally, that means every character sits at a leaf and no character sits at an internal node along the way to another. Therefore the first leaf you reach is unambiguously the end of exactly one character — you never need to look ahead or undo a step. This is the property that makes the simple 'stop at the first leaf' rule correct.

**Why reset matters.** Forgetting to reset to the root after an emit is the classic bug: the pointer would keep descending from the leaf (which has no children), either crashing on a null move or silently producing garbage. Resetting restarts the next codeword from the top of the tree.
approaches.insight: The encoded string is a tape of turn-left / turn-right instructions, and the prefix-free tree guarantees each character's instructions end precisely at a leaf. Decoding is therefore a single linear pass with a reset — no heap, no lookahead, O(1) space.

dryRun.intro: Pointer starts at root. '0'=left, '1'=right. Emit and reset on each leaf.

code.python:
# Definition for a Huffman tree node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, freq, data):
        self.freq = freq
        self.data = data      # meaningful only at leaves
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def decodeHuff(root: Node, s: str) -> None:
    out = []
    node = root
    for bit in s:
        node = node.left if bit == '0' else node.right   # 0=left, 1=right
        if node.left is None and node.right is None:      # leaf reached
            out.append(node.data)
            node = root                                   # reset for next code
    print(''.join(out))

approaches.name: Prefix-Table Decode — Build code→char Map First
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as an alternative or when you'll decode many strings against the same tree and want a reusable lookup.
hints: Traverse the tree once, accumulating the path ('0'/'1') to each leaf, to build a code→character dictionary.
Then scan the encoded string, accumulating bits until the running prefix matches a code in the dictionary.
Because codes are prefix-free, the first match is unambiguous — emit, clear the buffer, and continue.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the table visits all N tree nodes → O(N). Decoding scans L bits, each appended and checked in O(1) average against the map → O(L). Total O(L + N); the map costs O(N) space.
approaches.explanation:
Instead of walking the tree per bit, precompute the dictionary once and then match prefixes in the string.

**Build the codebook.** DFS the tree carrying the path string built so far: append `'0'` going left, `'1'` going right. At each leaf, record `code → character` in a map. This single traversal captures every codeword.

**Decode by prefix matching.** Walk the encoded string accumulating bits into a buffer. After each bit, check whether the buffer matches a key in the map. The prefix-free property guarantees that as soon as the buffer equals some code, it can't be the prefix of a different code, so the match is unambiguous — emit that character, clear the buffer, and keep scanning.

**Trade-offs versus the tree walk.** This uses O(N) extra space for the map and O(N) preprocessing, so for a single decode the direct tree walk is strictly simpler and lighter. The table shines when you decode *many* strings against the *same* tree: you build the map once and reuse it, and the per-string cost is O(L). It also generalizes to non-binary tries. Functionally the two produce identical output because both rely on the same prefix-free structure.
approaches.insight: The tree walk and the prefix table are the same algorithm wearing different clothes: both exploit prefix-freeness so the first complete codeword is unambiguous. Pick the table only when amortizing the build across many decodes; otherwise the O(1)-space tree walk wins.

code.python:
def build_codes(node, path, codes):
    if node is None:
        return codes
    if node.left is None and node.right is None:   # leaf
        codes[path or '0'] = node.data
        return codes
    build_codes(node.left, path + '0', codes)
    build_codes(node.right, path + '1', codes)
    return codes

def decodeHuff(root: Node, s: str) -> None:
    codes = build_codes(root, '', {})
    out = []
    buf = ''
    for bit in s:
        buf += bit
        if buf in codes:                           # prefix-free -> first match is final
            out.append(codes[buf])
            buf = ''
    print(''.join(out))

Check if the current bit buffer exactly matches a codeword.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to reset the pointer to the root after emitting a character.
Emitting characters at internal nodes instead of only at leaves.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No reset after emitting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After hitting a leaf you must restart at the root. Without the reset the pointer tries to descend from a childless leaf — a null move (crash) or garbage on subsequent bits.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Emitting at internal nodes
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Internal nodes are structural and their data field is a placeholder. Emitting there produces placeholder characters in the output; only leaves hold real data.

node = (bit == '0') ? node.left : node.right;
out.append(node.data);   // wrong: appends even at internal nodes

patternNote: Decode a prefix-free code by walking a binary tree under external instructions: bits choose left/right, leaves are emit points, and a reset-to-root after each leaf starts the next codeword. The prefix-free property guarantees unambiguous single-pass decoding in O(L) time and O(1) space; a precomputed code→char table is the reuse-friendly variant.
